title: Subject-Identity Removal Does Not Improve Frozen EEG Foundation Model Transfer: A Negative Result

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to systematically test whether removing linearly decodable subject identity improves cross-subject transfer of frozen EEG foundation model embeddings. This specific objective — improving cross-subject transfer by removing subject-specific information — is not directly addressed in any prior paper. While many papers (e.g., [3], [7], [9], [15], [28]) discuss cross-subject EEG transfer or domain adaptation, none explicitly focus on the removal of linearly decodable subject identity as a mechanism to improve transfer. Papers like [5], [22], and [27] discuss concept erasure or debiasing, but they do not apply this to EEG embeddings or cross-subject transfer.

### Mechanism
The mechanism combines Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP) with Euclidean Alignment (EA) preprocessing and inner-cross-validation hyperparameter selection under a leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocol with linear probing. INLP is explicitly introduced in [5], where it is described as a method for removing linearly encoded information from neural representations. EA preprocessing is not explicitly mentioned in any prior paper, but LOSO protocols are discussed in [24] and [26]. The combination of INLP with EA preprocessing and LOSO is novel, as no prior paper combines these specific techniques for EEG embeddings.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves systematic testing on BNCI2014001 motor imagery data (9 subjects, 22 channels) with 3 seeds, comparing INLP-CV against an EA baseline. The evaluation design uses LOSO cross-validation, which is explicitly covered in [24] and [26]. The use of a specific dataset (BNCI2014001) and comparison against EA does not make the evaluation design novel, as the LOSO protocol and systematic comparison framework are established methods.

### Domain
The domain is EEG brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) for cross-subject transfer in motor imagery. This domain is extensively covered in prior papers, including [1], [3], [4], [6], [9], [15], [23], and others. While the specific dataset (BNCI2014001) and focus on frozen embeddings may be narrower, the general application area of EEG-based BCIs for motor imagery is well-established.
